analysis.one_liner: Gives people exposed to PFAS "forever chemicals" a federal right to sue makers for medical monitoring.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it sat in two House subcommittees from April 2021 until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let people significantly exposed to PFAS — man-made "forever chemicals" used in nonstick cookware, waterproof clothing, and many manufacturing processes — sue the companies that made or processed those chemicals in federal court, alone or as a class. The main remedy would be court-ordered medical monitoring: periodic check-ups to catch PFAS-linked diseases early, paid for by the responsible companies rather than the exposed person. It also set a presumption of exposure for people with PFAS in their blood, and it died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People significantly exposed to PFAS, including the roughly 200 million Americans whose drinking water the bill's findings say contains the chemicals, plus communities near manufacturing sites and exposed workers. Today they have no federal statutory claim for PFAS exposure; the bill would give them one, along with a presumption of exposure when PFAS shows up in their blood, and would shift the cost of exposure-related medical testing onto the companies responsible.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal cause of action letting significantly exposed individuals — or classes of them — sue any company that made the PFAS they were exposed to, or whose manufacturing process created it, in any U.S. district court.

Authorizes courts to award medical monitoring: periodic diagnostic exams, beyond what a person would otherwise get, when significant exposure raises the risk of a PFAS-linked disease such as cancer, shifting those costs from the exposed person to the responsible party.

Sets a presumption of significant exposure when a person's blood test shows PFAS, or when the defendant's process released PFAS into an area the person was exposed to for at least a year — and makes the defendant pay for the testing if it wants to rebut that presumption.

Where there is not enough toxicological data to prove a disease risk, courts may lower the scientific proof standard and order companies to fund new epidemiological or toxicological studies, addressing the research gap the bill's findings say industry has left unfilled.
Preserves all state-law claims and remedies, so the new federal claim would be an addition, not a replacement, for existing lawsuits.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and other companies whose processes created PFAS, including toll and telomer manufacturers, would bear litigation costs, the cost of rebuttal blood testing, court-ordered research, and medical monitoring awards. Some of those costs would likely be passed to customers through prices.

drawbacks.text: Liability would reach far beyond the original chemical makers: any company that engaged in 'any portion of a manufacturing process that created the PFAS' — including telomer, fluorosurfactant, or toll manufacturing — could be sued, sweeping many downstream firms into class actions.

Courts may lower the standard of scientific proof for disease risk when toxicological data is insufficient, meaning liability and court-ordered studies could rest on unsettled science until better data exists.

The remedy is monitoring, not cleanup or treatment: the bill does nothing to remove PFAS from drinking water or soil, and the cost of treating any disease that does develop would still fall on the exposed person.

A person needs only 'reasonable grounds to suspect' significant exposure to file, which lowers the bar for starting a lawsuit and could generate substantial litigation even for people never actually exposed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people carrying PFAS in their blood with no federal way to hold anyone accountable, the bill offered a real remedy — early detection paid for by the companies that made the chemicals. The costs fall on a concentrated industry, though they are real: broad liability that reaches downstream manufacturers, claims built on a lowered scientific standard, and pass-through price effects. The bigger design gap is that medical monitoring does not clean up contamination or pay for treatment, so the bill treats the symptom of exposure, not the contamination itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees, never got a hearing or a vote in either, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Madeleine Dean introduced the PFAS Accountability Act on April 22, 2021, with nine Democratic cosponsors.

The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees the same day, and within two days both had sent it to subcommittees — Environment and Climate Change, and the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote. The bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
People exposed to PFAS were left with the status quo: no federal statutory cause of action for PFAS exposure, with only state-law claims available.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and the broader set of companies whose processes create PFAS came out ahead — they avoided a new federal lawsuit avenue and mandatory medical monitoring and research costs for the life of the Congress. Exposed people gained nothing.

for.name: Madeleine Dean
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill, writing the findings on PFAS in the blood and drinking water of Americans.

for.name: 9 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Judiciary Chairman Jerrold Nadler, whose committee nonetheless never acted on it.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on introduction and referred it to the Environment and Climate Change Subcommittee, where it stayed without a hearing or markup for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, but his committee referred it to a subcommittee in October 2021 and never brought it to a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, but no committee or floor vote ever happened, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have exposed these companies to federal class actions from significantly exposed individuals, mandatory medical monitoring awards, and court-ordered toxicological studies they would fund. Because the bill died, they kept the status quo in which exposed people have no federal statutory claim.

industries.industry: Downstream manufacturers using PFAS in their processes (e.g., nonstick cookware, weatherproof apparel, toll manufacturing)
industries.note: The bill's cause of action covers any company that engaged in 'any portion of a manufacturing process that created the PFAS,' so these firms would have faced the same class-action exposure as the original chemical makers. Avoiding that liability is their gain from the bill's death.
